world.bio: Thai-British documentary producer based in Bangkok. I have produced two broadcast nature documentaries and I am now developing a personal feature film about the Mekong giant catfish and the river my grandfather fished. I live in a half-renovated shophouse in Talat Noi with my husband and teenage son.
skills_assets: Fifteen years in documentary production; credits on two broadcast nature films
A relationship with a European public broadcaster's commissioning editor and a development budget
A pitch slot at a regional documentary forum in March 2027
A small network in Thai, Lao and Cambodian fishing communities through my late grandfather
Production office space above a noodle shop in Talat Noi

projects.name: The Last Giants (working title)
projects.text: A feature documentary on the collapse of Mekong giant catfish fishing, told through three generations of one fishing family. The broadcaster I'm talking to likes the story but has said they want 'data and sound, not just faces'. That means real river data, not only interviews, and a sound world that feels like the river itself. I have a pitch slot at a regional doc forum in March 2027 and still no upstream (Chinese) perspective, which the commissioning editor flagged as the missing half of the story.

projects.name: Shophouse renovation
projects.text: Our family house in Talat Noi is being renovated: new wiring, a proper kitchen, and a rooftop office. It is three months behind schedule and over budget.

notes.text: Skype call with the commissioning editor, Anneke. She said the story is moving but the film is a portrait without an argument. 'Data and sound, not just faces,' she said. I wrote that on a sticky note and put it above the monitor. It feels like a challenge and a kindness at the same time.

My grandfather's old photographs are scattered in boxes. One of them shows him with a catfish bigger than himself on the bank near Chiang Khong. 1987, the back says. I scanned it three times, each time slightly different. The fish is taller than the boy standing next to it.

Renovation chaos. The plumber found an old well under the kitchen floor. My husband says it's a sign. I say it's a budget line. We both laughed, then I cried a little in the car because the contractor wants another 80,000 baht.

My son said at dinner that he wants to leave the international school and study online. He says nothing there matters. I did not shout. I said we'd talk after the weekend. I know I'm doing what my parents did to me: postponing the difficult talk.
Played futsal on Sunday, scored two, strained my hamstring. The team is mostly twentysomethings who call me 'Auntie Ploy.' I pretend not to mind.

Wrote a rough treatment for the pitch. The structure works: downstream collapse, upstream dams, the fishermen in between. But I only have one side of the river. Who tells the upstream story? Not as villains. As engineers, scientists, people on the same water. I need that voice, otherwise the film is a lament and not an investigation.
Found a note from the forum: submissions close in January; the pitch slot is in March 2027. I have six months to turn a promise into a package. Anneke's budget covers development only.

Went up to the roof of the shophouse at night. Bangkok never gets dark, but the river is there, brown and slow, passing under the lights. I thought of my grandfather's hands, and the way he talked about the river as if it were a person.

messages.text:
Anneke: Ploy, the treatment is lovely. But I want to see the river as a system.
Me: Understood. I'm looking for hydrological data and a way to record the soundscape.
Anneke: Good. Data and sound, not just faces.
Me: Yes.

Tom: Contractor called again about the well.
Me: I'll handle it tomorrow.
Tom: You always say tomorrow.
Me: This time I mean it.

Nok: Grandpa's catch notebooks are still in my mother's house.
Me: Can you photograph them?
Nok: Of course. But not today, the monsoon flooded the lower road.
Me: No rush, just keep them dry.

Kit: Mum, can I do school online?
Me: Let's talk Saturday.
Kit: You said that last week.
Me: I know. I'm sorry.

Hana: Please confirm your pitch slot for March. We need the working title.
Me: The Last Giants.
Hana: And the team?
Me: Still forming.

relations.about: British, works in logistics, patient, frustrated about the renovation.
Lives near Chiang Khong, has grandfather's old things.
Commissioning editor at a European public broadcaster; direct, supportive, strict.

constraints: Budget only covers development until pitch
Limited access to Chinese-language sources and contacts
Cannot film in China without proper permission
sensitive: Anxiety about delivering the film in time for the pitch
Strained family time because of work and renovation
Worry about her son's school unhappiness
